title: Turning what you built into something you can hand over
promise: You'll package your project so someone else can understand it, use it and maintain it without you: which files make it up, which document explains it and what exactly gets handed over. By the end you'll have the handover folder done.
why: Nuria finished her system and wanted to show a colleague so she could set up the same thing. She sent her a WhatsApp with screenshots and said «it's easy, you do it with Claude». The colleague tried for three afternoons and gave up. It wasn't that it was difficult: it was that what Nuria had in her head wasn't written down anywhere. Her project existed inside her and inside an account. Outside that it didn't exist, and that's why it could neither be taught nor charged for.

theory.title: A project that only works with you standing there isn't finished
theory.text: This is the line separating a personal setup from a piece of work. As long as only you use it, everything you know by heart makes up for what isn't written down: what had to be switched on, why that odd step is there, what happens when the other thing fails. The moment another person has to use it, or you yourself in eight months, that memory isn't there and the setup falls over. Packaging isn't paperwork to look good: it's what turns something that works into something that exists outside your head. And it's exactly what gets assessed when you show it, defend it or charge for it.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between cooking well and having a recipe. Cooking well feeds your family. With the recipe written down, someone else cooks the dish and you can sell the book.
theory.example: Nuria's system worked perfectly. What didn't exist was any way for it to work without her.

theory.title: The five things you hand over
theory.text: A complete handover has five pieces and none of them is long. First, the setup itself: the exported workflows, the code, the configurations. Second, the one-page document saying what problem it solves, for whom, and what's needed for it to work. Third, the start-up instructions: the exact steps, with button names, to bring it up from nothing. Fourth, what you already have from the previous block: the checks, the undo plan, the breakdown log. And fifth, the limits: what it's for, what it isn't for, and what has to be watched. That fifth is the one that inspires the most confidence and the one almost nobody includes.
theory.example: Nuria's handover folder: the workflow exports, README.txt, START-UP.txt, the checks and breakdowns folder, and LIMITS.txt. Five things.

theory.title: The page that gets read before anything else
theory.text: Every handover starts with a one-page document, and it has to answer four questions in this order: what problem it solves, for whom, what you need to have for it to work, and what happens when you start it up. No architecture and no technology on that page: that comes later. What whoever opens it is after is whether this is any use to them, and they decide in thirty seconds. Write it last, when you have everything, but put it first in the folder.
theory.example: «Solves: searching 192 accounting practice documents and answering with the file cited. For: a small practice with documents in PDF and Word. You need: a Claude Pro account and the documents cleaned up. On start-up: you ask in ordinary language and it answers with the source beside it.»

theory.title: The start-up gets written while you do it
theory.text: The universal mistake with instructions is writing them from memory. What comes out are instructions that work only for someone who already knows, because they skip the steps you do without thinking. The only way to write them properly is to run the process from scratch while writing them, noting every click with the name that appears on screen. And then the real test: someone else following them without you saying a word. Every time that person asks something, you have a missing step. That isn't a failure on their part, it's your list being incomplete.
theory.example: «Go into n8n» is a step written from memory. «Open n8n.yourcompany.com, sign in with your account, press the + button top right and choose Import from File» is a step written while doing it.

theory.title: Written limits inspire more confidence than promises
theory.text: It works the opposite way to intuition: saying what your project isn't for makes whoever receives it trust you more, not less. A handover promising it solves everything smells of never having been tested. One saying «it's accurate at this, that has to be checked by hand, and it's no use for this other thing» reads as the work of someone who knows what they've built. And besides, you already have those limits written down if you've done the earlier blocks: they're in the «what-its-for» file from block 07 and in the checks from block 08.
theory.example: «It's no use for accounts or adding up amounts. Official deadlines always have to be confirmed by hand. Scanned documents with no text can't be queried.»

theory.title: The handover itself, which is where everything falls apart
theory.text: There's a part of the handover that isn't a file and that decides whether the project survives: who maintains it, on which accounts, and what happens when something fails. If you're handing it to a client, the accounts and the keys have to be theirs, not yours, or the day you part ways everything stops. If you're the one keeping it running, that gets written down too: what it covers, what it doesn't and how you get told. It's the awkward conversation everyone avoids at the start and that turns out expensive later.
theory.example: «The OpenAI and n8n accounts are in the client's name. Maintenance: I review once a month and fix breakdowns within 48 hours. Doesn't include new features.»

tasks.title: Build the handover folder
tasks.action: Create a folder named after your project and inside it five subfolders or files with these exact names: «1-README.txt», «2-START-UP.txt», «3-SETUP» (with the exported workflows and code), «4-CHECKS» (what you did in block 08) and «5-LIMITS.txt». The numbers in front make them sort themselves into the order they should be read in.
tasks.expect: The structure created, with folders 3 and 4 already filled if you did the earlier blocks. The three text files empty for now.
tasks.stuck: If folder 4 is empty because you skipped block 08, go back to lessons 35 and 37: they're the checks and undo files. Without those, the handover doesn't stand up.

tasks.title: Write the page that gets read first
tasks.action: Four sections, one page at most. What problem it solves (with a real example, not an abstract one). Who it's for and who it isn't for. What you need to have before starting: accounts, paid plans, documents, permissions. And what happens when you start it up, told as whoever uses it would see it.
tasks.expect: One page. Test it: give it to someone who knows nothing and ask whether they understand what it's for. If they take more than a minute to know, shorten it.
tasks.stuck: If it's coming out long, you're explaining how it works inside. That goes in the start-up. Here only what it solves and what you need.

tasks.title: Write the start-up by doing it
tasks.action: This gets written while building, not from memory. Start from nothing, as though you had none of it, and note each step as you take it: which site you go to, which button you press and what it's called on screen, what you type, what you have to see to know that step worked. That last detail is what makes instructions followable without you.
tasks.expect: A numbered list where each step has the action and what you see when it's done. Between ten and twenty-five steps is normal.
tasks.stuck: If you can't build it from scratch because you already have it built, do it on a test account or with a duplicate. And if that isn't possible, write it and mark it: «steps written from memory, untested». At least whoever reads it knows where they stand.

tasks.title: Gather the limits you already have written
tasks.action: Don't write it from scratch: copy it from where it already is. The what-it's-for-and-what-it-isn't file from lesson 34. The acceptance criteria from lesson 35. What you can't do with the data, from lesson 41. The monthly cost from lesson 42. And the approval points from lesson 44. Put it all in one file with five sections.
tasks.expect: A file gathering what you already knew, in one place. If gathering it reveals a gap (you don't know what it costs a month, say), that gap has to be filled before handing over.
tasks.stuck: If those files don't exist because you skipped those blocks, write them now even if briefly. A handover without written limits is the one that causes arguments three months later.

tasks.title: Have someone follow it without you saying a word
tasks.where: With a person who doesn't know the project
tasks.action: This is the acid test. Give someone the folder and ask them to try starting it up following only what's written. You sit beside them and say nothing, only noting each time they stall or ask. Don't help, not even with gestures.
tasks.expect: A list of between three and eight points where they got stuck. Each one is a missing or badly explained step. Add them and repeat with someone else if you can.
tasks.stuck: If nobody can do it, do it yourself in a week's time, following the instructions to the letter and without using what you remember. It's worse than a fresh person, but it uncovers a fair amount. The rule: if you have to think, a step is missing.

tasks.title: Write the handover terms
tasks.action: Four awkward and necessary lines: whose name the accounts and keys are in, who maintains this from now on, what that maintenance includes and what it doesn't, and how you get told when something fails. Write it even if the project is only yours: in a year, that «yours» may have changed.
tasks.expect: Four lines. If you're handing it to a client, this is what prevents the argument six months from now about who pays for the account and who fixes the breakdowns.
tasks.stuck: If the accounts are in your name and the project belongs to a client, change it before handing over. It's easier now than when there's data inside and workflows running.

matters: That a project which only works with you standing there isn't finished.
That a handover is five pieces and none of them is long.
That the instructions get written while building, not from memory.
That writing the limits inspires more confidence than promising it solves everything.
ignore: Documenting the internal architecture. Nobody reads it and it doesn't help anyone start this up.
Writing a long manual. One page and a list of steps return far more.
Pretty diagrams before the instructions actually work.
canDo: Hand over a project another person can bring up without you.
Explain in one page what it solves and what's needed.
Spot the missing steps by watching someone follow your instructions.
Leave in writing who maintains what and on which accounts.
cantDo: Hand over something you haven't tried building from scratch.
Stop whoever receives it misusing it if you don't write the limits.
Replace a setup that doesn't work with documentation.
Hand over accounts in your name without changing them first.
words: The complete bundle: setup, explanation, start-up, checks and limits.
The exact steps to bring it up from nothing, with the names as they appear on screen.
What it's for, what it isn't and what has to be watched. What inspires the most confidence.
Whose name the accounts end up in and who maintains the project after handover.
Watching a person follow your instructions without helping. The only way to know what's missing.
next: You have the package. In lesson 46 you learn to show it: how to tell a project in five minutes so people understand what it solves, without starting from the technology.
